cues.text: Receivables are money customers still owe: just over $11 million.
It picks ten customers, by size and by risk.
A confirmation is a letter the customer answers straight to the auditors. Eight reply, and three differ from the books.
Two customers stay silent. One has since paid; one has not.
It explains each difference. A $28,600 credit was never recorded, and one customer hasn't paid since December.
Last, it weighs the findings against materiality, the size of mistake that matters, and writes the workpapers for the CPA.

All done. The one known mistake is the $28,600 credit, well under materiality. Add two judgment calls, about $41,000 held back by a customer and up to about $187,000 that may never be paid, and the total passes the auditors' working limit. Seven items stay open. The CPA, a person, concludes and signs. The machine gives no opinion.
